newsitem.title: USA: White House to move quickly on trade legislation.
newsitem.headline: White House to move quickly on trade legislation.

text.p: The White House plans to move quickly to win legislative authority from the new Congress to negotiate a wider North American Free Trade Agreement to include Chile, a senior trade official said Tuesday.
The so-called "fast track" trade negotiating authority "is one of the early issues we will be taking up," Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat told a trade conference.

Eizenstat said he expected a difficult negotiation with congressional leaders, but that he believed the administration could win sufficient support for legislation that will give U.S. trade officials authority to negotiate trade deals without fear they will later be changed by Congress.

"It will be difficult, it will be contentious, but my grounds for at least guarded optimism are that ... when push comes to shove, there has always been a bipartisan majority in favor of trade liberalization," Eizenstat said.

The legislation would also allow U.S. trade officials to negotiate other trade arrangements including the Free Trade Agreement of the Americas pact that would unite the hemisphere into a single trading bloc by 2005.

Eizenstat said he hoped the administration will have made substantial progress in winning Congressional passage of the fast track legislation by the time the hemispheric trade ministers meet in May in Belo Horizonte, Brazil.

The fast track legislation has taken on new urgency since Canada signed its own trade pact with Chile this week. NAFTA is comprised of Canada, the United States and Mexico, and U.S. officials are anxious to bring Chile into the trade agreement.

But efforts to win Congressional passage of fast track authority failed last year because of a dispute between the Clinton administration and Republicans, who control Congress, over authority to negotiate labor and environmental issues in trade deals. Eizenstat said he was confident a deal could be made with the new Congress, which is to begin in January.

"We believe there is a deal that can be made," Eizenstat told reporters after a speech to a European Institute conference. "It will take a lot of negotiation with congressional leaders, but we believe this is something that can be achieved and that will be achieved."

But House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt, who opposed congressional approval of Mexico's entry into NAFTA in 1993, warned administration officials on Monday that expansion of NAFTA would be unacceptable if key issues were not addressed, including labor and the environment.

"I don't think we ought to just extend NAFTA to other countries," Gephardt told a news conference. "Before we enter such a treaty with other countries in Central and South America, we ought to get the improvements that we've been looking for. If the Chileans are willing to make those improvements, I see no reason not to do that."
